description: The chip makers, the big cloud companies and the newer rented-computing firms, data centres and the power they draw, memory and networking.

economics.case: NVIDIA and AMD take [fact:chips_gp_share] of the gross profit (sales minus the direct cost of making them) that this site can measure across chips, one cloud and the leading labs; that share is up on the year, though it slipped in the latest quarter. Yet chips from other designers already make up [fact:silicon_share_now] of the AI computing shipped so far, including custom chips that Broadcom and others build for large cloud and model companies. TSMC's filing calls its scale and capacity, particularly for advanced processes (the newest generations of chip-making, which print the smallest features), a major competitive advantage, and its biggest customers as a group have taken a larger part of its revenue each year since 2023, even as its single largest customer's share fell. ASML says it is currently the world's only maker of extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, which print the finest features with light of a very short wavelength, and that one supplier, Carl Zeiss, makes all their optics and limits how many it can build. Against this unit, this site reads foundry supply as easing: TSMC's capacity is catching up with demand. That undercuts the title's claim for the foundry only if the easing reaches TSMC's own prices and margins, which this site cannot yet see, since TSMC files under international accounting rules this site's filing reader does not read. The three designers' own conditions do not collide: NVIDIA's, Broadcom's and AMD's can all hold at once until chips from other designers make up most of the AI computing shipped.
economics.commoditising: Chips made on older processes are cheap and interchangeable; TSMC's own filing says rivals in those processes are numerous. This site judges that the cost of a unit of computing keeps falling with each chip generation, and that the general-purpose AI chip is being copied from below: every large buyer that designs its own chip, often with Broadcom's help, turns part of NVIDIA's market into a price to negotiate. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products.
economics.converts_if: For the designer: its software (for NVIDIA, CUDA, the platform developers write AI code against) and its whole-rack systems with their own links between chips keep buyers even when rival chips are plentiful and cheaper, turning a shortage rent into switching costs, what a customer would lose by moving to a rival. For the foundry and the toolmaker: they keep a lead at each new process, so their scale and process power outlive the AI shortage.
economics.kill_shot: NVIDIA keeping both its share of AI chip supply and its gross margin while AMD's chips and the custom chips ship in volume and wafer supply at the newest processes keeps growing fast; or a second foundry making AI chips at the newest process in volume for a major designer.
economics.mechanism: Three kinds of firm make AI chips. Designers such as NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom draw them; a foundry (a factory that makes chips to other firms' designs), above all TSMC, prints them onto wafers (thin discs of silicon, each later cut into many chips); and toolmakers such as ASML build the machines that do the printing. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. So while buyers cannot get enough chips, the designer they most want takes the rent. This site judges that as more chips arrive and the biggest buyers design their own, that rent is exposed, while the foundry and the toolmaker keep theirs for as long as no rival can match what they do.

rival.title: Some link in the chip chain proves easier to expand

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that capacity at the newest processes, and the machines that print it, stay scarce. A new factory for the newest process takes years to build and the skill to run it takes longer. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier, and named the kinds that recur. Two apply here: process power (a way of working that takes rivals years to learn) and scale economies (unit costs that fall as volume grows, so a rival must match the volume to match the cost). The EUV machines have one maker, fed by one optics supplier: a cornered resource, Helmer's term for preferential access to something others need, which does not ease when chips do.
economics.title: The chip designer's lead is a shortage profit; the foundry's and the toolmaker's are harder to copy

economics.case: SK hynix reported record results for 2025, with HBM revenue growing sharply and demand for ordinary server memory rising sharply too. Samsung describes low inventory and supply constraints in memory. This site's tightness word for memory reads moderate, though memory is counted in dollars, so a price rise looks like more memory. Micron's own filing warns that if HBM demand weakens and makers shift capacity back to ordinary DRAM, its supply could rise sharply, and that an oversupplied market pushes prices down; it also names Chinese state-backed makers, CXMT and YMTC, among the causes of that risk.
economics.commoditising: Ordinary memory, the kind in phones and laptops, is a textbook commodity: identical parts, several makers, and prices that swing with each wave of new factories. Networking built to open standards such as Ethernet, which Broadcom sells to the largest cloud and model companies, is interchangeable by design. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part, and David Ricardo, an English economist who studied why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. On their account the rent in memory lasts only until the makers build their way out, and SK hynix says it is building new factories in Korea.
economics.converts_if: Custom HBM, memory built to one buyer's design, which SK hynix calls a key differentiator, becomes the norm, so each chip generation is locked to one maker and switching costs replace the shortage. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than rivals, named switching costs, what a customer would lose by moving to a rival, as one of the lasting advantages he found. In networking, the rent lasts only if NVIDIA's own links stay faster than open standards by enough that buyers accept being tied to one vendor.
economics.kill_shot: Memory makers keeping record margins through a year in which all three add HBM capacity faster than AI chip shipments grow and ordinary memory prices fall.
economics.mechanism: An AI chip is only as fast as the memory that feeds it. High-bandwidth memory, or HBM, is DRAM (the working memory a processor reads and writes constantly) cut into dies (single chips), stacked and placed beside the processor so data reaches it quickly. This site counts three makers: SK hynix, Samsung and Micron. Micron's filing says HBM needs more wafers (the silicon discs chips are cut from) and more factory space than ordinary DRAM for the same amount of memory, so when AI demand runs ahead the makers profit, and if it weakens they can turn the same factories back to ordinary memory. Networking, the switches, cables and light-based links that join many chips into one machine, splits in two: NVIDIA's own links, which tie buyers to its systems, and gear built to open standards, which any maker can supply.

rival.title: Computing cannot flood the market overnight

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the skill to stack dies with good yield (the share of units that work) and to be qualified (tested and approved) by a chip designer for its next product; a newcomer would need both, and this site judges they take longer to learn than one product generation. NVIDIA's own links between chips stay scarce because only NVIDIA makes them, though its filing says it now lets other firms' chips connect to them.
economics.title: High-bandwidth memory is a cyclical commodity earning a shortage's price

economics.case: This site reads electricity as severe and data-centre buildings as tight, though the electricity reading measures only how fast demand grows, not supply. The biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue, so money is not what is short; this site reads capital as slack. TSMC's filing names constraints in power supply among the things that could slow demand for its chips. Against this unit, power generated on site beside the data centre, and chips that do more work for each unit of electricity, would both loosen the grid's hold. The wait to be connected is the gauge that would show the shortage directly, and this site knows of no public series for it.
economics.commoditising: This site judges that the building itself, the shell, the racks and much of the cooling, follows standard designs that many contractors can put up, and that money for the build-out is plentiful. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs an innovation needs to reach its customers complementary assets; generic ones, which anyone can buy, earn an ordinary return, not a rent.
economics.converts_if: Holders of connected sites and running power stations lock their buyers into long contracts at prices set during the shortage, or regulators let utilities earn a guaranteed return on new lines built for data centres, turning a shortage rent into a regulated one. It fails to convert if power built on site, beside the data centre and off the grid, proves quick and cheap.
economics.kill_shot: New large sites being connected to the grid about as fast as they are built, with the rent for powered data-centre space falling while use keeps rising.
economics.mechanism: A data centre needs three things: a building, money, and electricity delivered through a grid connection. This site judges that buildings and money can be had quickly, while a new connection means waiting for the utility to add lines and transformers, and new power stations take years. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part; David Ricardo, an English economist who studied why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. So, in this site's judgement, the rent goes to whoever already holds land with power and a connection. Much of that input sits with utilities whose prices a regulator sets, so they cannot charge what the shortage is worth; this site judges that the rent leaks instead to owners of connected sites and of power stations already running.

rival.title: The spending runs ahead of the revenue, and investors take the loss

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that grid connections, heavy electrical gear such as large transformers and turbines, and the electricians and other trades who install them stay scarce. A connection is close to a licence: a utility grants it under a regulator's rules and it cannot be copied, which makes it what Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied lasting advantages, calls a cornered resource: preferential access to something others need. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who studied contracts and found that a buyer who depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would expect the largest buyers to own such assets or lock them up in long contracts.
economics.title: A site already wired to the grid is scarcer than the building or the money

economics.case: The big clouds' own segment profits are high: this site's filed figures show AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft's cloud segment each earning a high operating margin (profit after running costs, as a share of sales), one that moves up and down from quarter to quarter. Oracle's filing says some of its cloud offerings are concentrated among a number of large customers, and that some customers may be heavily in debt. Their spending runs far ahead of AI's revenue: the biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue. Microsoft's remaining performance obligations (revenue customers have signed for but not yet received) stand at [fact:msft_backlog] its revenue over the past year, against [fact:msft_backlog_year_ago] a year before. The clouds also fund their own customers: Microsoft's filing calls it a major investor in OpenAI with rights to OpenAI's models, and Amazon's filing records investments in Anthropic and a large gain on them in 2025. Microsoft warns that overestimating demand could leave its data centres underused and force it to write down their value (cut the value it records for them). Amazon lengthened the working life it assumes for its servers in 2024, then shortened it for some servers and network equipment in 2025, citing how fast AI technology moves. Oracle set up a programme to sell new shares into the market over time, but had sold none by the end of May 2026. On the neocloud side, CoreWeave's filing says its largest customer, Microsoft, gave it most of its revenue in 2025, that OpenAI and Meta have signed large contracts, that customers commit to take-or-pay contracts (they pay for the capacity whether or not they use it), and that it finances its infrastructure mainly with debt secured on those contracts. Nebius says the long contracts it signed with Microsoft and Meta came with financing terms that let it grow, while most of its customer contracts so far have been short. The hourly rent for NVIDIA's previous-generation flagship chip changed by [fact:h100_rent_yoy] over the past year on this site's latest reading (a minus sign would mark a fall).
economics.commoditising: This site judges that an hour on a given GPU is becoming a commodity: the same NVIDIA chips are rented by many firms, Nebius names CoreWeave, Crusoe and Lambda as well as the big clouds among its rivals, and CoreWeave says its customers specify NVIDIA's chips, so the chip, not the cloud, is what they are buying. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices. On that finding, the rent on each generation of chips falls towards cost as those chips become plentiful. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets. This site judges that a neocloud's rack of rented chips is a generic one, which anyone with money, power and a supply of chips can assemble; the scarce inputs behind it belong to others, NVIDIA's chips on one side and the demand of a few big buyers on the other.
economics.converts_if: The big clouds turn chip rental into services customers build on, such as their own chips, their own model catalogues and the tools that run AI inside a firm's data, so switching costs hold AI work as they hold older work. For a neocloud: long take-or-pay contracts with buyers who can pay, signed during the shortage, outlast it, and it wins powered sites others cannot get, a cornered resource in Helmer's term (preferential access to something others need). Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by its owner, would expect the biggest buyers to build their own capacity once they can, which is the risk a neocloud's contracts must outlast.
economics.kill_shot: Big-cloud margins falling to the neoclouds' level as AI becomes most of what they sell, with customers moving AI work between clouds on price alone; or a neocloud keeping its margin through a year in which GPU rents fall steeply and its largest customer leaves at the end of its contract.
economics.mechanism: A cloud rents out computing by the hour or by the contract. The big clouds, often called hyperscalers (Microsoft's Azure, Amazon's AWS, Google Cloud and Oracle), sell AI chips alongside storage, databases and the software businesses already run on them. The neoclouds (newer firms such as CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda and Fluidstack that rent out mostly NVIDIA's graphics chips, GPUs, and little else) sell the chips almost alone. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that a neocloud's margin is that kind of rent, the gap between what a scarce chip rents for and what it costs to buy, power and borrow against, and that it lasts while chips and powered buildings are short; a big cloud's margin rests more on customers whose data and systems already sit inside it.

rival.title: The builders overbuild and rent out the rest

economics.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is powered, connected data-centre space and, for the big clouds, the customer relationships and the data already stored with them. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Scale economies and switching costs apply to the big clouds' existing business today: scale economies (unit costs that fall as volume grows, so a rival must match the volume to match the cost; Google offers its own AI chips, TPUs, beside GPUs) and switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival, here the work of moving data and systems built around one cloud). This site judges that neither is yet proven for AI work in particular, which is younger and easier to move than the systems firms have run in the cloud for years.
economics.title: The big clouds keep a rent from customers who stay; the neoclouds earn the shortage's price on borrowed money

name: Compute & physical

profiles.customers: A small group of chip makers: the leading logic foundries and the memory makers. The filing does not name them, but says its largest customer's share of its sales rose in 2025 and that its sales lean heavily on its two largest customers. The rankings shift from year to year.
profiles.market: ASML sells lithography machines, the tools that print a chip's circuit pattern with light onto a wafer (a thin silicon disc later cut into chips), plus the service, upgrades and software that keep them running. Its most advanced line uses extreme ultraviolet light (EUV, light of a very short wavelength that can print the finest features). Its newest EUV design, High-NA (optics that gather more light, to print still finer features), has gone mostly to customers' research sites, and the filing says ASML has now released its first full-specification High-NA machine to its first customer. The filing says ASML is currently the world's only maker of EUV machines, and names Canon and Nikon as rivals only in the older deep-ultraviolet machines. Its buyers are chip factories making logic (processors) and memory. In 2025 its logic sales grew, driven by foundries (factories that make chips to other firms' designs) building for AI demand, while its memory sales fell; sales of older machines in China were stronger than it expected. ASML files a 20-F (the annual report foreign companies file with the US regulator) under IFRS, the international accounting rules, so this site's filing reader records no figures for it.
must_be_true: The world keeps building factories for the newest processes (the latest generations of chip-making, which print the smallest features) in logic and memory faster than old ones retire, so demand for EUV machines grows rather than just replacing worn tools.

Chip makers keep shrinking features with lithography rather than with other processes that would need fewer of its machines; the filing names competition from alternative technologies or manufacturing processes only in general terms.
High-NA EUV reaches mass production and customers adopt it on the finest layers, so the next generation is also ASML's alone.
Zeiss and ASML's other single-source suppliers can grow output fast enough that their capacity does not cap its sales for years at a time.
Export rules between the United States, the Netherlands and China do not shut it out of a large block of buyers while a state-backed rival learns to build competing machines.
profiles.name: ASML

powers.why: An exclusive arrangement with Carl Zeiss SMT, its sole supplier of optics, in which ASML holds a stake, and no EUV rival named in its own filing; this site judges the benefit is pricing and the barrier is the long joint optics work a rival would have to repeat.
This site judges that each EUV generation takes years of research spread over every machine sold, so a rival would need the same volume of sales to carry the same cost.

Customers design their factory processes around its machines and buy its service and upgrades for years after; its service and upgrade sales grew faster than machine sales in 2025, though the filing says part of that came from upgrades to installed EUV machines being counted there instead of as machine sales.

rent.reads: a monopoly-like profit, kept by the company itself

would_disprove: A rival, including a state-backed Chinese maker, shipping working EUV-class machines to a paying customer's factory.
Leading chip makers delaying or skipping High-NA for the finest layers and staying with older EUV plus extra patterning steps (printing the same layer more than once).
Its largest customers cutting orders for new EUV machines while AI chip demand still rises, showing the factories were built ahead of need.
New export rules removing China from its buyers without other regions making up the older-machine sales.

profiles.customers: Its ten largest customers account for a large part of revenue, and the 10-K singles out one unnamed customer, mostly served by the cloud memory unit, as a large buyer. Customers are generally reluctant to sign long fixed-price contracts, so prices and volumes are renegotiated as the market moves. A 2023 Chinese government ruling bars operators of critical information infrastructure in China from buying its products.
profiles.market: Micron makes memory chips: DRAM (the working memory a processor reads and writes constantly), NAND (the storage that keeps data when power is off) and high-bandwidth memory, or HBM (DRAM dies, single chips cut from a silicon wafer, stacked and placed beside an AI chip so they can feed it data very fast). It sells to cloud firms, server makers, phone and PC makers and car makers, and reorganised in 2025 around business units, one of which serves the largest cloud buyers and holds all its HBM sales to data centres. Memory has long been a cyclical, commodity market: its 10-K (the annual report US companies file with their regulator) warns that an oversupplied market pushes prices down, and that heavy investment, including by Chinese state-backed makers, threatens oversupply. This site's filed figures show the swing: Micron made a gross loss (sales below the direct cost of making them) in 2023, and has since swung from losses to a gross margin, the share of sales kept after those costs, among the highest this site has recorded for it. How big the market becomes depends on whether AI keeps memory short, and for how long.
must_be_true: AI keeps raising the amount of memory each unit of computing needs, so memory demand grows faster than the makers can add capacity, cycle after cycle.

HBM stays a different product from ordinary DRAM, bought on stacking skill and a long qualification (testing and approval) with each chip designer rather than on price per bit, the smallest unit of stored data.
Micron keeps pace with SK hynix on each new HBM generation, including HBM4, instead of arriving after the best prices are gone.
The memory makers do not all add so much capacity at once that the old glut returns.
Chinese state-backed makers such as CXMT do not reach the newest processes and flood ordinary DRAM with cheap supply.
profiles.name: Micron

powers.why: Emerging, not proven. This site judges that a memory factory at the newest process costs so much that only a few firms can build one; the benefit holds against newcomers, but not against Samsung or SK hynix, which build at the same scale or larger.

rent.reads: a thin profit, kept by incumbent firms

must_be_true: micron_10k_fy25

would_disprove: Memory prices and Micron's gross margin falling back toward their 2023 lows while AI spending is still rising.
Chip designers buying HBM on price alone and moving volume freely between suppliers from one generation to the next.
Micron's HBM4 reaching volume later than its rivals' or failing a major customer's qualification.
The memory makers' combined spending on new factories rising far faster than the growth in memory bits shipped.

profiles.customers: The results post names no customers and gives no concentration figures. It describes demand from AI memory and from server memory and storage. That a few AI chip designers buy most HBM is this site's judgement from the market's shape, not from this source.
profiles.market: SK hynix makes DRAM (the working memory a processor reads and writes constantly), NAND (storage that keeps data when power is off) and high-bandwidth memory, or HBM (DRAM dies, single chips cut from a silicon wafer, stacked and placed beside an AI chip so they can feed it fast). Its own results post for 2025 says record results came from AI memory, that its HBM revenue grew sharply, that demand for ordinary server memory also rose sharply, and that it was the first in the industry to complete the preparations to mass-produce HBM4, the next generation, while still supplying the previous one. It is building new factories in Korea and advanced packaging plants (where chips and memory are mounted together) in Korea and Indiana. It files no reports with the US regulator, so this site records no filed figures for it; its only source here is that short post, which is the company describing itself, not an audited filing. This site judges memory to be historically cyclical and commoditised, and a record year says nothing on its own about the next downturn.
must_be_true: Its lead in HBM survives each new generation, so it keeps being among the first suppliers qualified (tested and approved) by the biggest AI chip designers.
Custom HBM, memory built to one buyer's design, which its post calls a key differentiator, becomes common, turning a lead in yield into switching costs that outlast any single shortage.
AI keeps memory demand ahead of the makers' capacity, so memory prices do not fall back to their old cycle.
Its new factories and packaging plants come online without it and its rivals overbuilding at the same time.
Its largest AI chip customers keep growing and do not spread their orders evenly across the memory makers.
profiles.name: SK Hynix

powers.why: Emerging, not proven. Its post says it was the first in the industry to be ready to mass-produce HBM4 and supplies both current generations at once; this site judges the benefit is earlier orders at the best prices, and the barrier is how long it takes to learn to stack dies with good yield (the share of units that work).
Emerging, not proven. This site judges it one of three firms with DRAM factories at the newest processes; the cost of a new factory keeps newcomers out, though not its two peers.

rent.reads: a thin profit, kept by incumbent firms

must_be_true: skhynix_fy25_results

would_disprove: Samsung or Micron qualifying HBM4 with the largest AI chip buyer at the same time and in similar volume.
HBM prices per unit falling from one generation to the next while demand still grows.
Its operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, falling back to the levels of an ordinary memory downturn while AI spending is still rising.
Custom HBM staying rare, with buyers treating HBM as interchangeable between makers.

profiles.customers: The report lists its major customers across the whole company, alphabetically: Alphabet, Apple, Deutsche Telekom, Hong Kong Techtronics and Supreme Electronics. It does not break out the buyers of its memory or HBM, which this site judges are far more concentrated than the company as a whole. The one long contract it lists is Tesla's, for foundry work.
profiles.market: Samsung Electronics is a conglomerate. Its chip division makes DRAM (working memory), NAND (storage) and high-bandwidth memory, or HBM (DRAM dies, single chips, stacked beside an AI chip so they can feed it fast), designs phone processors and camera sensors, and runs a foundry (a factory that makes chips designed by others). It also makes phones, televisions, home appliances, displays and car electronics. Its business report for 2025 says that, with low inventory and supply constraints in memory, it expanded HBM sales, and that it aims to supply HBM4 for new AI chips, both graphics processors and custom ones. The same report, citing the research firm DRAMeXchange, shows its share of world DRAM revenue falling in both 2024 and 2025. It signed a foundry contract with Tesla running to 2033. Samsung files no reports with the US regulator, so this site records no filed figures for it; its source here is its English business report.
must_be_true: It closes the HBM gap with SK hynix and is qualified (tested and approved) in volume by the largest AI chip designers for HBM4 and after.
AI keeps memory short for long enough that its large capacity earns scarcity prices rather than dragging prices down.

Its foundry wins more outside designs at the newest processes (the latest generations of chip-making), like the Tesla contract, so that it becomes a real second source, an alternative supplier buyers can switch orders to, to TSMC for AI chips.
Buyers value getting memory, foundry work and packaging (mounting chips and memory together) from one firm enough to pay for it.
Ordinary consumer electronics, a large part of its sales, do not absorb the gains from chips.
profiles.name: Samsung Electronics

powers.why: Emerging, not proven. This site judges it one of three firms with DRAM factories at the newest processes, with cash from phones and appliances to keep building through a downturn; the barrier holds against newcomers, less so against SK hynix.

rent.reads: a thin profit, kept by incumbent firms

source_links.label: Samsung Electronics business report, year to 31 Dec 2025

must_be_true: samsung_report_2025
skhynix_fy25_results

would_disprove: Its share of world DRAM revenue falling further while memory is still short.
The largest AI chip designers qualifying HBM4 from SK hynix and Micron but taking little or none from Samsung.
Its foundry failing to win another large outside customer for its newest processes.
Memory prices falling back to their old cycle while AI spending is still rising, as its own large capacity comes online.

profiles.customers: The filing lists cloud providers, newer specialist clouds it calls neoclouds, model makers, companies and governments. Most chips reach them through server makers and assemblers, so the direct customers are middlemen. In the year to January 2026 its largest direct customer and its second largest each took a large part of revenue, and the filing says some indirect buyers, reached through those channels, were also each large enough to disclose. This site judges that those end buyers are largely the same few companies designing chips of their own.
profiles.market: NVIDIA designs accelerators, chips built to do the huge number of simple sums that training and running AI models needs, mostly graphics processors (GPUs). It sells them as chips and as whole server racks, with the networking gear that ties many of them together and the software developers write their code against (CUDA, its programming platform). It does not make the chips itself: foundries, factories that make chips to other firms' designs, make its wafers (the silicon discs chips are cut from). Its filing says it brings out a new data-centre architecture every year. How big it can become depends, in this site's judgement, on how long the big buyers keep raising their spending on AI data centres.
must_be_true: Spending on AI data centres by the largest cloud and platform companies keeps rising into the 2030s instead of being cut back after a stretch where AI revenue fails to cover it.

Chips the big buyers design themselves (Google's, Amazon's, Meta's, and those Broadcom builds for them) stay a minority of AI computing shipped, so NVIDIA's buyers cannot replace it with their own designs.

NVIDIA's gross margin stays well above AMD's and Broadcom's after supply of chips, packaging and memory catches up with demand, which would show the rent (profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off) rests on software lock-in and not only on shortage.
Software that lets the same model code run on any chip does not make the choice of chip a matter of price alone.

It keeps first call on the leading foundry's newest process and on advanced packaging (mounting the chip and its memory together on one base), and that foundry keeps operating in Taiwan without interruption.
Export controls stop short of shutting it out of markets beyond China, and a China-only product line is not the price of staying in the rest.
Its own lending, guarantees and equity stakes in customers stay small next to sales, so demand is paid for by buyers and not by NVIDIA's balance sheet.

powers.why: Years of AI code, tools and staff skills are written for CUDA, so moving to another chip means rewriting and retesting; this site's filed figures show the benefit in a gross margin (the share of sales left after the direct cost of making them) well above AMD's even as rivals shipped.

This site judges that as one of the largest buyers of wafers, advanced packaging and memory it spreads a very large research budget over the most units, and that a new architecture every year is a pace a smaller rival cannot fund from its own sales.

The second is infrastructure software, mostly VMware, which lets a company run many virtual computers on its own servers. Its semiconductor segment, the chip business it reports separately, brought in most of its revenue in the year to November 2025. Ethernet, an open standard, stays the way AI clusters are wired, rather than NVIDIA's own networking.

This site judges it the main other seller of general-purpose AI accelerators besides NVIDIA, and that its AI market is whatever share buyers give to a second source, an alternative supplier they can switch orders to: large if buyers want to stop depending on one supplier, small if NVIDIA and custom chips split the market between them.

Taiwan keeps supplying enough electricity and water for new factories, which the filing lists among its risks.

David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns from what they invent, found that the firm holding the complementary assets (the distribution, sales and systems a product needs to reach buyers) often keeps the profit; this site judges that Microsoft holds its own: its data centres and its customers.

profiles.market: Microsoft sells software and cloud services. It also sells AI inside products businesses already pay for, such as its office software and GitHub. OpenAI keeps growing, pays what it has committed, and keeps much of its computing on Azure; the filing lists OpenAI as a related party and warns that partners who are big Azure customers may change their purchasing.

profiles.market: Alphabet sits in two parts of the chain. As a cloud, Google Cloud rents computing, storage and AI services, offering both graphics processors (GPUs) and its own tensor processing units (TPUs, chips Google designs for the maths AI models run on; the filing names Ironwood as its seventh generation), plus Vertex AI, a platform for building on its Gemini models and other companies' models, and Workspace office software. As a frontier lab (a company building the most capable AI models), it develops the Gemini models, which the filing says run across all of its largest consumer products, including Search through AI Overviews and AI Mode. The filing says the cost of developing its general AI models sits in Alphabet-wide costs rather than in the Google Cloud segment, and that cloud margins are generally lower than advertising margins. It spent heavily on capital (buildings and equipment) in 2025 and said it expected to raise that spending significantly in 2026. This site's filed figures show the Google Cloud operating margin (the share of sales left after running costs) rising sharply over the past year from the lowest among the big clouds. This site judges its market is both renting AI computing and selling AI inside its most widely used consumer products, and that owning chips, models and distribution together is rare.
must_be_true: Gemini stays among the most capable models, so Alphabet does not have to pay another lab for the models that run its own products.

Companies it invested in and also sells cloud services to stay solvent and pay, and the credit backstops it has given to data-centre entities are not called.
Its capital spending earns back before the equipment ages out; the filing warns that expected technology advances could change the period over which it benefits from these assets.

It has since signed multi-year contracts to provide dedicated GPU capacity to Microsoft, at a new site in New Jersey, and to Meta; both contracts give the buyer service credits (discounts owed when service falls short) or the right to end tranches (separate portions of the deal) if delivery is late. One Meta order obliges Meta to buy any capacity in certain clusters that Nebius fails to sell to other customers. Its largest customer took a large part of 2025 revenue, and one customer owed most of its receivables (money customers owe it) at the end of 2025. It relies on NVIDIA for its GPUs and named a strategic partnership with NVIDIA in March 2026. It funds itself with convertible notes (loans that can turn into shares), share sales, and advance payments from these large contracts. This site judges that the racks it rents out are a generic asset, which anyone with money, power and a supply of chips can assemble; the scarce inputs behind its business belong to others, NVIDIA's chips on one side and the demand of a few big buyers on the other.
profiles.market: Nebius is a neocloud, a newer cloud built to rent out AI computing. It rents clusters of NVIDIA graphics processors (GPUs), including the GB200 and GB300 systems, in a data centre it owns in Finland and in built-to-order or shared sites in the United States, Europe and Israel, and sells software on top, including Token Factory, which serves open AI models and charges by the token (a small chunk of text a model reads or writes) instead of by the GPU-hour. It also owns smaller businesses, among them Avride, a self-driving developer. The company was called Yandex N.V. until 2024, when it sold all its businesses in Russia, which were almost all of the group at the time, and kept the AI cloud and a few smaller units. It files a 20-F (the annual report foreign companies file with the US regulator), but prepares its accounts under US accounting rules. This site holds filed figures on its debt, including its total debt and borrowing rates, but no filed revenue or capital-spending figures for it. This site judges its market is AI computing for customers the big clouds do not serve first, plus overflow capacity for the big clouds themselves.
must_be_true: It earns a lasting advantage it does not hold today, for example if Token Factory and its other software turn it from a renter of chips into a platform customers would lose work by leaving.

It delivers the Microsoft and Meta capacity on schedule; the filing says it has limited experience delivering contracts this large and that late delivery lets those buyers claim credits or end tranches (portions of the contract).
It wins enough other customers that its dependence on a few big clouds shrinks as their contracts run down.
Capital stays available on terms its contracts can carry while it spends ahead of revenue.
The price of renting GPUs does not fall faster than the cost of owning, powering and financing them.
The big clouds and labs do not build enough of their own capacity to stop needing neoclouds.

profiles.market: Fluidstack is a neocloud (a newer company that rents out AI computing power, competing with the large clouds of Amazon, Microsoft and Google). In November 2025 Anthropic chose it to build data centres custom-made for Anthropic's work in New York and Texas, with more sites to come and the first coming online during 2026; it says Anthropic chose it for how fast it can deliver gigawatts of power (a gigawatt is a very large amount of electric power, about what a big power station produces). Anthropic keeps paying for the sites built for it; Oliver Williamson, who studied why firms own assets tied to a single partner, found that such assets invite a fight over price once they are built, and a data centre made for one customer is that kind of asset.

profiles.customers: It names no customers; it says it designed with leading AI companies, cloud providers and hyperscalers (the largest cloud companies). This site judges its early contracts come from a few buyers.
profiles.market: Etched designs systems for inference (running a trained AI model to answer requests) on the largest models: its own chips, plus the racks (cabinets holding many chips wired together), cooling, power supply and software around them, designed together. Its chip is a kind of ASIC (an application-specific integrated circuit, a chip built for one kind of work rather than general use). It says its first chip came back from TSMC, the contract chip maker, earlier in 2026, that it is testing its first rack-scale product with customers, and that it has begun production against customer contracts. It claims design advances: running its maths circuits at low voltage so they can work harder without overheating, and a memory design that mixes HBM (high-bandwidth memory, stacked beside the chip to feed it fast) with SRAM (very fast memory built into the chip) and pools it across chips. It has opened a factory in Taiwan. How big the market becomes depends on whether buyers want a specialised inference machine once NVIDIA and the clouds' own chips also chase inference.
must_be_true: Its racks deliver, in customers' data centres, the throughput, speed of response and power savings it reports from early tests.
Inference becomes a large enough share of AI spending, and the leading models' designs stay stable enough, that a specialised machine beats general chips.

It gets enough capacity from TSMC and the memory makers; this site judges they serve NVIDIA and the large clouds first, though Etched says it is deepening its partnership with the leading chip manufacturer and has a strategic investment from VentureTech Alliance.
Its customers buy beyond first orders, and NVIDIA's and the clouds' own chips do not close the gap first.
